JMPR: Total dithiocarbamates, determined as CS2, evolved during acid digestion and expressed as mg CS2/kg
EU:
Reg. 396/2005: Dithiocarbamates expressed as CS2, including maneb, mancozeb, metiram, propineb, thiram and ziram
Peer review (EFSA, 2020a): Dithiocarbamates (mancozeb) determined and expressed as CS2
efsa_comments:
It is noted that in the context of the recent MRL review under Art. 12 of Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 (EFSA, 2023e), EFSA proposed the following residue definitions applicable for plant and animal products:
RD enf: dithiocarbamates (dithiocarbamates determined and expressed as CS2, including maneb, mancozeb, metiram, propineb, thiram and ziram)
RD RA: (1) mancozeb (analysed as CS2 and expressed as mancozeb)
RD RA: (2) ETU
For enforcement purposes the EU and JMPR residue definitions are comparable. To express the residues of mancozeb as CS2, the molecular weight conversion factor of 1.78 is applicable.
For risk assessment purposes the residue definitions differ as the RD set by the JMPR includes metabolite ETU, which, according to the JMPR assessment, is 7.5 times more toxic than parent compound. Therefore, to express residues of ETU as mancozeb toxicity equivalents the ratio of the ADIs of mancozeb and ETU (7.5) is used by the JMPR.
In the EU, ETU is included in a separate residue definition, to be assessed against the TRV derived for ETU.

EU:
Reg. 396/2005: Sulfoxaflor (sum of isomers)
Peer review (EFSA, 2014d):
Sulfoxaflor
The residue is not fat soluble
efsa_comments:
The residue definitions for enforcement set by JMPR and at EU level are substantially identical, since the ISO common name sulfoxaflor covers the two diastereomeric pairs of enantiomers of sulfoxaflor.
At EU level, the residue definition for risk assessment in plant and animal commodities is more comprehensive and includes the metabolite X11719474. X11719474 is a plant and soil metabolite, which has shown to be preferentially taken up by the roots of the plants and to be present (> LOQ) in the leafy parts of the crops in rotation crops, particularly in feed items.
The EU pesticide peer review considered metabolite X11719474 to be quantitatively relevant in primary and rotational crops (EFSA, 2014d). However, its inclusion in the residue definition for risk assessment of plant and animal products was provisional. Lacking toxicological data on the metabolite, currently exposure assessments are performed, assuming that this metabolite is as toxic as the parent compound.
The EU pesticides peer review agreed that if metabolite X11719474 is shown to be significantly less toxic than sulfoxaflor, the residue definition for the risk assessment should be revised to parent sulfoxaflor only.

Sum of parent sulfoxaflor and metabolite X11719474, expressed as sulfoxaflor
If metabolite X11719474 is shown to be significantly less toxic than sulfoxaflor, the residue definition for risk assessment will become parent sulfoxaflor only.
efsa_comments:
The residue definitions for enforcement set by JMPR and at EU level are substantially identical, since the ISO common name sulfoxaflor covers the two diastereomeric pairs of enantiomers of sulfoxaflor.
At EU level, the residue definition for risk assessment in plant and animal commodities is more comprehensive and includes the metabolite X11719474. X11719474 is a plant and soil metabolite, which has shown to be preferentially taken up by the roots of the plants and to be present (> LOQ) in the leafy parts of the crops in rotation crops, particularly in feed items.
The EU pesticide peer review considered metabolite X11719474 to be quantitatively relevant in primary and rotational crops (EFSA, 2014d). However, its inclusion in the residue definition for risk assessment of plant and animal products was provisional. Lacking toxicological data on the metabolite, currently exposure assessments are performed, assuming that this metabolite is as toxic as the parent compound.
The EU pesticides peer review agreed that if metabolite X11719474 is shown to be significantly less toxic than sulfoxaflor, the residue definition for the risk assessment should be revised to parent sulfoxaflor only.

EU: Reg. 396/2005: Quinclorac
efsa_comments:
In 2017, the EU submitted a concern form regarding the residue definition, because quinclorac methyl ester which is 10 times more toxic than quinclorac was not included in the residue definition for enforcement, noting that quinclorac methyl might be used as a variant of the a.s. quinclorac in plant protection products (to be confirmed by the manufacturer of the a.s.).
The EU concern was addressed by JMPR in 2018: JMPR confirmed the previously derived residue definition, highlighting that the overall exposure was low.
The EU reserved its position to include quinclorac methyl ester in the EU residue definition for enforcement for rapeseed, considering the higher toxicity of the methyl ester.
EFSA still has concerns that the RD for enforcement does not cover the more toxic variant quinclorac methyl ester, but acknowledges that the inclusion of a variant for which no data were submitted to JMPR is not in line with the JMPR assessment practice.

The residue is fat soluble

Reg. 396/2005: Spiromesifen
MRL review (EFSA, 2019a): Inconclusive (No residue definition proposed in the absence of appropriate metabolism studies)
Peer review (EFSA, 2012f): Not proposed
The residue is not fat soluble
efsa_comments:
The current residue definitions for enforcement established in Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 are not directly comparable with the residue definition proposed by JMPR which comprises also the enol‐metabolite. In the framework of the MRL review, the enol‐metabolite was proposed to be included in the residue definition for enforcement, but recommendations of this assessment have not yet been legally implemented.
As regards the risk assessment residue definition (RD‐RA), for plants, JMPR proposed to include not only the enol‐metabolite but also 4‐hydroxymethyl‐Sp‐enol, free and conjugated; the latter was not proposed by the peer review. In the framework of the Article 12 MRL review, two RD‐RA were proposed: (1) primary crops, except leafy crops including spiromesifen‐enol (M01) and (2) for leafy and rotational crops, also including enol (M01), spiromesifen‐4‐hydroxymethyl (M02) and its conjugate M03. It was noted that the inclusion of metabolites M04 and M06 in the residue definition for rotational leafy crops may need to be reconsidered, based on the outcome of a rotational field trial on succeeding leafy (EFSA, 2019a).
Since the proposed Codex MRLs are for fruits and pulses and oilseeds only, for which the RD‐RA is the same in the EU and JMPR, the difference in the RD‐RA derived by JMPR and the EU (for leafy crops and rotational crops) will not have an impact on the assessment.
It is noted that for animal products, residue definitions at the EU level could not be proposed in the absence of appropriate metabolism studies. There are no Codex MRL proposals for livestock commodities.

efsa_comments:
The EU and JMPR enforcement residue definitions for plants are nearly identical, covering only parent fenazaquin. In the EU, for risk assessment, a second residue definition was established for metabolite TBPE. Overall, EU residue definitions for both enforcement and risk assessment for plants are restricted to fruit crops while JMPR derived a global enforcement residue definition. Furthermore, the risk assessment RD for plants derived by JMPR was not used for the risk assessment of pulses and leafy vegetables, as it was derived from metabolism studies in two crop groups (cereals and fruit). Hence requests for setting CXLs for pulses and mint were rejected.

The RMS informed EFSA that during the renewal of the approval, the residue definitions for plant products (enforcement and risk assessment) are confirmed (still restricted to fruits). The previous tentative residue definition for leafy vegetables is no longer supported by the RMS.
The residue definitions for ruminants are also confirmed during the renewal, but the RMS highlighted that the representative uses do not include feed items and therefore they are not required.

EU:
Reg. 396/2005: Afidopyropen (default MRLs/RD according to Art. 18(1)(b))
No EU peer review and no MRL review
efsa_comments:
Plant products: In metabolism studies, parent afidopyropen was the major compound in the majority of primary crop commodities (up to 61% TRR). However, in soya bean, parent afidopyropen was detected at very low concentrations in dry soya bean seed (0.4% TRR, 0.001 mg/kg). The metabolite trigonelline (M031) identified in soya bean seeds (47% TRR) is also a naturally occurring alkaloid in many plants. The dimer M007 was found in dry soya bean seeds at 1% TRR and 12% TRR, depending on the study.
Animal products: Parent afidopyropen was the major compound in animal tissues, ranging from 17% TRR in goat kidney to 97% TRR in egg yolk and up to 6.8% TRR in milk. The ester cleavage metabolite M001 was a major metabolite in milk, liver, kidney and muscle, ranging from 24% to 66% TRR, and was also a minor metabolite in fat (4.6% TRR). M017 was a major metabolite in hen liver. The metabolic pathways in goat and hens are similar to that which is reported in rat.
CPCA is a metabolite that is formed by cleavage of the cyclopropane carboxylic acid ester moieties from the parent molecule. Parent afidopyropen contains two CPCA groups. From livestock and rat metabolism studies it is known that metabolism can lead to the cleavage of only one or both CPCA ester moieties. Including CPCA in the residue definition (expressed as parent compound) seems problematic, since one molecule of afidopyropen may generate 1 or 2 molecules of CPCA. Hence the molecular weight conversion factor to recalculate the amount of CPCA to afidopyropen equivalents could be either 6.9 or 3.45. Hence, this leads to ambiguous results.
In 2021 CCPR, the EU expressed concerns on the appropriateness of the risk assessment residue definitions derived by JMPR, as the inclusion of CPCA in the residue definition for risk assessment may lead to ambiguous results.
According to the results of the livestock metabolism and feeding studies, parent compound was below the LOQ while the levels of the total residues (parent +M001 + CPCA‐carnitine expressed as parent) was more than 20 times higher. Hence, parent compound is considered not a valid marker substance and therefore the RD for enforcement should be reconsidered for muscle/meat and milk.

efsa_comments:
JMPR identified the following information missing that would be desirable to derive proposals for enforcement residue definitions for plant and animal products:
Submission of the metabolism data in alfalfa
Identification of major unknown components in all plant matrices from broccoli, maize and peanut metabolism studies
In the EU assessment the RMS suggested in the RAR with respect to the non‐identified metabolites that these metabolites of higher polarity are not relevant since they are intermediates in of the natural detoxification process with no biological activity and no potential for accumulation.

EU:
Reg. 396/2005: Mefentrifluconazole
Peer review (EFSA, 2018g): Mefentrifluconazole (BAS 750 F)
efsa_comments:
Plant commodities: In the primary crop metabolism studies conducted in grape, soya bean and wheat, mefentrifluconazole was the predominant compound in most of matrices (60–92% TRR) in forage (wheat, soya bean), leaf/stalk (grapevine), straw/hull/chaff (wheat, soya bean), green pod (soya bean) and grape (grapevine). In wheat grain and soya bean seed, mefentrifluconazole was present at very low levels, while TDMs (triazole metabolites, mainly triazole alanine) represented the predominant residues.
In a rotational crop metabolism study in leafy vegetables, root and tuber vegetables and cereals, mefentrifluconazole and TDM were identified as major residues, similar to the primary crops.
The ratio of R‐ and S‐enantiomers of mefentrifluconazole residues in plants remained unchanged compared with the test substance.
The residue definitions for enforcement and risk assessment derived by JMPR and at EU level are identical. However, in the EU, additional risk assessment residue definitions comprising the TDMs were set.
Animal commodities:
In goat matrices, parent mefentrifluconazole and 1,2,4‐triazole were the predominant components of the residue. Significant change in the ratio of S:R enantiomers was revealed in most of goat matrices with proportion of the R‐enantiomer of 70–80% in cream, muscle, liver, kidney and fat. A similar shift was observed in liver and kidney of rats.
In poultry matrices, the metabolite M750F022 (and its fatty acid conjugates) is the predominant component of the residue, with parent mefentrifluconazole and 1,2,4‐T also present as significant components.
Based on this data JMPR proposed the RD for enforcement as mefentrifluconazole (free and conjugated);
At EU level, the residue definition for enforcement only comprises the parent compound (without the conjugates).
EFSA considers the RD for enforcement derived by JMPR not appropriate, because
The individual conjugates are not sufficiently defined; to develop and validate enforcement methods, the individual components need to be available as analytical standards to check if the method is capable to analyse for them (e.g. efficiency of hydrolytic step to convert the conjugate to the unconjugated form).
Currently, no analytical methods are available for enforcement,
The conjugates of the parent compound are of minor relevance;
The parent compound is therefore considered to be an appropriate marker substance.
For risk assessment the JMPR and the EU RD are not comparable, as JMPR also included the conjugates of the parent compound (see discussion of RD for enforcement) and M750F022 (and its conjugates) for all animal products. As the samples of animal products derived in the feeding studies were not analysed for the conjugates, JMPR derived correction factors from the metabolism studies.

EU: Reg. 396/2005: Tetraniliprole (default MRLs/RD according to Art. 18(1)(b))
efsa_comments:
The active substance was never assessed at the EU level – residue definitions have not been proposed at the EU level.
In the plant metabolism studies involving foliar applications (apples, potato, lettuce, paddy rice), soil drench application (tomato), granular in planting hole applications (rice) and seed treatments (potato and maize), in confined rotational crop metabolism studies and in processing studies, tetraniliprole was the major component (apple, tomato, lettuce, tomato, potato) of the radioactive residue. It was noted that apart from one outdoor study in maize and another in potatoes (seed treatment in furrow), all studies were conducted indoor. However, the JMPR concluded that the indoor studies sufficiently cover outdoor uses (since photodegradation was, at the most, only a minor path of degradation of tetraniliprole in soil).
Tetraniliprole is found in all primary crop commodities and is considered suitable as a marker compound. The JMPR decided to define the residue for compliance with the MRL as tetraniliprole.
Metabolite tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BSC‐CQ63359) was the only compound identified in relevant amounts in plant matrices. This metabolite was found at up to 20% TRR in tomato, rice grain and potatoes, but generally at levels ≤ 0.01 mg eq/kg in food commodities. This occurrence was confirmed in the supervised field trials, in which it was only found occasionally above the LOQ of 0.01 mg/kg, with tetraniliprole being present at levels about an order of magnitude higher.
Tetraniliprole is not stable under baking/brewing/boiling (pH 5, 100°C, 60 min) and sterilisation (pH 6, 120°C, 20 min) conditions. Under these conditions 65–68% and 1.1–1.5% AR was recovered as parent and 27–30% AR and 94% AR as tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BSC‐CQ63359), respectively. Processing under heating indicated conversion of parent tetraniliprole into tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BSC‐CQ63359), e.g. mustard greens (up to 20% TRR), broccoli (up to 29% TRR), tomato paste (23–48% TRR) and soya bean meal (up to 81% TRR).
The JMPR concluded that tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BSC‐CQ63359) may occur in primary and rotational crops and that the metabolite contributes significantly to the residue in processed commodities. Hence the JMPR agreed to define a residue definition for dietary risk assessment for plant commodities as tetraniliprole and tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BSC‐CQ63359), expressed as tetraniliprole.
Metabolism in animals was assessed in goat and poultry studies. Tetraniliprole was a major component in all goat tissues (24–71% TRR), poultry fat (26–55% TRR) and eggs (4.2–14% TRR), but it contributes little to the overall residue in poultry muscle (3.7–10% TRR) and liver (1.6–4.2% TRR). Metabolite tetraniliprole‐despyridyl‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone was a major compound in eggs and fat (63% TRR, 0.029 mg eq/kg) and was also found in liver (12% TRR, 0.065 mg eq/kg) and muscle (8.6% TRR, 0.001 mg eq/kg). Parent tetraniliprole was also the major component in all cattle tissues and milk. Therefore, the JMPR decided to define the residue for compliance with the MRL as tetraniliprole.
In deciding which compound should be included in the residue definition for dietary risk assessment, the JMPR noted that the tetraniliprole was metabolised into numerous components, of which 17 were accounted for > 10% TRR and/or > 0.01 mg eq/kg.
The metabolites were considered in three categories, either covered by the toxicity of the parent, suitable for assessment by the TTC approach following Cramer Class III or by the TTC approach for genotoxic compounds.
Based on the assessment of metabolites, the JMPR proposed the residue definition for dietary risk assessment for animal commodities as follows: sum of tetraniliprole, tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BSC‐CQ63359) and tetraniliprole‐benzylalcohol (BCS‐CZ91631), expressed as tetraniliprole.
EFSA does not fully agree on the residue definition for animal products. In particular, for poultry, parent tetraniliprole seems to be not a good marker substance and therefore the residue definition for enforcement is considered not appropriate.
In addition, tetraniliprole‐despyridyl‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone was found to be a the major compound in eggs (36% TRR, 0.030 mg eq/kg) and fat (63% TRR, 0.029 mg eq/kg); it was also found in liver (12% TRR, 0.065 mg eq/kg) and muscle (8.6% TRR, 0.001 mg eq/kg).
In the toxicological evaluation of 2021 JMPR, this metabolite (tetraniliprole‐despyridyl‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone) was reported to give alerts for genotoxicity using OECD QSAR ToolBox, Version 4.5.
In 2022, JMPR compared the exposure for this metabolite with the TTC Cramer class III threshold (see below JMPR risk assessment).
It is recommended to discuss with MS whether the proposed residue definitions for poultry are acceptable. Further details should also be checked in the JMPR evaluations, e.g. whether new information was available that allows to conclude that metabolite tetraniliprole‐despyridyl‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone does not have genotoxicity alerts.

EU: Reg. 396/2005: Inpyrfluxam (S‐2399) (default MRLs/RD according to Art. 18(1)(b))
efsa_comments:
The default residue definition for enforcement is parent only, which is same RD for enforcement derived by the JMPR.
The JMPR assessed plant metabolism studies performed with either [pyrazolyl‐14C] or [phenyl‐14C] labelled inpyrfluxam (JMPR 2022). Plant metabolism studies were conducted in apple and soya bean (foliar spray), rice (foliar and granular treatments) and maize, sorghum rapeseed and potato (seed treatment) at rates that accommodate the anticipated maximum total seasonal GAP application rates. The JMPR concluded that the metabolism was similar in all crops. The metabolism in rotational crops was similar to the metabolism observed in primary crops and the processing of inpyrfluxam is not expected to modify the nature of residues.
Inpyrfluxam was the predominant residue in apple (up to 79% TRR; 0.24 mg/kg), mature rice grain (up to 78.6% TRR; 0.039 mg /kg) and potato tubers (up to 15% TRR; 0.002 mg/kg) but was only found at very low concentrations in mature soya seed (up to 2% TRR; < 0.001 mg/kg). In feed commodities, parent was detected in soya bean forage (up to 50.5% TRR; 0.79 mg /kg), soya bean hay (up to 22.1% TRR; 0.5 mg/kg), immature pods (up to 65.2% TRR; 0.41 mg/kg), rice straw (up to 77.8% TRR; 0.72 mg/kg) and rice hulls (up to 52.5% TRR; 0.88 mg/kg). In the confined rotational crops study, parent was detected in mature lettuce (up to 26.9%; 0.027 mg/kg) and radish immature and mature roots (up to 58.9%; 0.045 mg/kg) at 30 to 365 days PBI.
The JMPR derived a residue definition for enforcement as parent inpyrfluxam only. Following consideration of the occurrence in plants and the toxicity of several metabolites, the JMPR decided that the residue definition for risk assessment should be inpyrfluxam only.
The metabolic fate of inpyrfluxam was investigated in lactating goats using [pyrazolyl‐14C] inpyrfluxam and [phenyl‐14C] inpyrfluxam for five consecutive days at 0.51 mg/kg body weight/day (13.74 ppm feed per day) for [pyrazolyl‐14C] inpyrfluxam and at 0.64 mg/kg body weight/day (15.74 ppm feed per day) for the [phenyl‐14C]inpyrfluxam and in laying hens using [pyrazolyl‐14C] inpyrfluxam and [phenyl‐14C] inpyrfluxam for seven consecutive days at 12.44 ppm feed per day for [pyrazolyl‐14C] inpyrfluxam and at 13.13 ppm feed per day for the [phenyl‐14C]inpyrfluxam.
In animal metabolism studies, inpyrfluxam was observed in poultry fat (up to 81% TRR; 0.075 mg eq/kg), goat fat (up to 15.8% TRR; 0.004 mg eq/kg) and eggs (up to 11% TRR; 0.002 mg eq/kg). In the feeding studies, parent was only present at 0.017 mg/kg in poultry fat from the highest dose group but not in any other animal tissue, milk or egg. Besides parent inpyrfluxam, metabolite 1′‐CH2OH‐S‐2840 (free or conjugated) was a major residue in most animal matrices and the predominant residue found in the livestock feeding studies.
Parent and metabolite 1′‐CH2OH‐S‐2840 residues were predominantly found in liver and kidney commodities.
In goats, concentrations between fat and muscle were close to the LOQ without clear tendency for accumulation in the fat. In poultry metabolism studies, fat contained approximately 30× higher residue concentrations compared to muscle. However, no accumulation was observed in milk fat or egg yolk. In the feeding studies, residues were generally low, not allowing estimation of ratios between fatty and non‐fatty tissues. The JMPR decided that the residue is not fat‐soluble.
The JMPR agreed that the residue definition for compliance with the MRL and dietary risk assessment for animal commodities should be: inpyrfluxam and 1′‐CH2OH‐S‐2840 (free or conjugated) expressed as inpyrfluxam.
At EU level residue definitions for risk assessment are not established for plants and animals since the substance was not yet evaluated in the EU.

Reg. 396/2005: Isoflucypram (default MRLs/RD according to Art. 18(1)(b))
Peer review (EFSA, 2022d): Isoflucypram (for all crop groups following foliar application)
efsa_comments:
At EU level, the same metabolism studies (primary crops, rotational crops and livestock) were assessed as by JMPR.
Overall, EFSA proposed parent isoflucypram as the residue definition for MRL enforcement for plant and animal products.
The risk assessment, residue definitions for animal products is provisional; the residue definition for risk assessment for plant products is limited to cereals only (EFSA, 2022d). The same residue definition as in primary crops was proposed provisionally also for rotational and processed commodities.
JMPR proposed only a residue definition for enforcement as isoflucypram for plant and animal products. For risk assessment, JMPR could not derive a conclusion on the residue definition due to the lack of genotoxicity studies for two metabolites found in rotational crop studies exceeding 0.01 mg eq./kg in mature Swiss chard (i.e. M52 and M54). The dietary exposure for these two metabolites was above the TTC for compound with potential genotoxicity.
Details on metabolism studies:
Primary crops: Metabolism studies in tomatoes, wheat, soya bean and rapeseed following foliar application and on root potatoes following the postharvest treatment. Isoflucypram was the major compound in all edible parts of the crops (max 93% TRR in wheat grain, 98% TRR in tomato fruits, etc) and in cereals feed items (up to 63% TRR in straw and 55% TRR in hay). Other relevant compounds found in relative and/or absolute amount were: M01 (isoflucypram‐propanol) and M06 (isoflucypram desmethyl propanol) free and conjugates in wheat straw and hay, in soya bean forage and hay were found also the M44 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐homo GSM), M45 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐Cys‐MA), M46 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐mercapto‐lactic acid‐OH), M47 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐mercapto‐lactic acid‐Glyc), M48 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐mercapto‐lactic acid – propil‐OH‐Glyc) and M58 (isoflucypram‐cyclopropyl‐pyrazole‐carboxamide) in potato tuber.
M01 and M06 free and conjugates were found in residue trials on cereals (i.e grains) at levels either comparable or higher than the parent.
Based on metabolism studies and field trials the residue definition for risk assessment at EU level was proposed as: sum of isoflucypram, M01 and its conjugates, M06 and conjugates expressed as isoflucypram limited to cereals only. For enforcement the residue definition was proposed as isoflucypram.
JMPR considered M01 could be excluded from the risk assessment based on the results from residue trials, due to the low occurrence of quantifiable residues in cereals; M06 was assess by using the TTC approach (Cramer Class III) and was found not relevant for risk assessment by JMPR.
In rotational crops, several compounds such as M49 (BCS‐CR60082), M52 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐N‐methyl‐cyclopropyl‐pyrazole‐carboxamide‐OH‐Cys) and M54 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐N‐methyl‐cyclopropyl‐pyrazole‐carboxamide‐OH‐GSH) occurred above 10% of TRRs, different than in primary crops. Isoflucypram was found only in wheat forage. For the metabolites M52 and M54, a potential concern for genotoxicity was identified at EU level. JMPR applied the TTC approach to assess M52 and M54, and concluded that the exposure was above the threshold for genotoxic compounds (0.0025 μg/kg bw per day).
Processing studies: Under standard hydrolysis conditions of pasteurisation, boiling/brewing/baking and sterilisation submitted during peer review isoflucypram and M01 are stable (98%). M06 degraded into M77 (isoflucypram‐desmethyl‐propanol‐aldehyde) under boiling/brewing/baking up to 66% and under sterilisation up to 98%). Since for M77 a genotoxicity potential could not be excluded, in the EU peer review process, a data gap was set to address genotoxicity, since the precursor substance M06 was found in barley grain at relevant levels.
Animal metabolism studies: Isoflucypram was found in all animal tissues, in milk and eggs, liver and ruminant fat. M01 and M06 were recovered at relevant amount in almost all matrices, except M01 in milk and ruminant fat. M07 (isoflucypram‐desmethyl‐1,2 propandiol), M11 ((isoflucypram‐desmethyl‐carboxylic acid) and M12 isoflucypram‐carboxylic acid) were found above 10% TRRs in poultry muscle and liver. However, based on poultry feeding studies M07, these metabolites were not expected above 0.01 mg/kg. In ruminants, additional compound such as M02 (isoflucypram‐2 propanol), M19 (conjugate of M01), M20 (conjugate of M02) and M50 were found as relevant; in the EU assessment, for M50 (isoflucypram‐N‐methyl‐pyrazole carboxylic acid) the genotoxicity potential was considered not addressed.
JMPR identified the following information missing that would be desirable to derive proposals for residue definitions for plant and animal products:
Submission of cereal grain processing data for isoflucypram‐desmethyl‐propanol (M06)
Hydrolysis of the extracts from soya bean metabolism studies
In the EU assessment, potential concerns for genotoxicity based on positive genotoxicity QSAR predictions were identified (M50, M66, M67, M77).

Animal metabolism studies: Isoflucypram was found in all animal tissues, in milk and eggs, liver and ruminant fat. M01 and M06 were recovered at relevant amount in almost all matrices, except M01 in milk and ruminant fat. M07 (isoflucypram‐desmethyl‐1,2 propandiol), M11 ((isoflucypram‐desmethyl‐carboxylic acid) and M12 isoflucypram‐carboxylic acid) were found above 10% TRRs in poultry muscle and liver. However, based on poultry feeding studies M07, these metabolites were not expected above 0.01 mg/kg. In ruminants, additional compound such as M02 (isoflucypram‐2 propanol), M19 (conjugate of M01), M20 (conjugate of M02) and M50 were found as relevant; in the EU assessment, for M50 (isoflucypram‐N‐methyl‐pyrazole carboxylic acid) the genotoxicity potential was considered not addressed.
JMPR identified the following information missing that would be desirable to derive proposals for residue definitions for plant and animal products:
Submission of cereal grain processing data for isoflucypram‐desmethyl‐propanol (M06)
Hydrolysis of the extracts from soya bean metabolism studies
In the EU assessment, potential concerns for genotoxicity based on positive genotoxicity QSAR predictions were identified (M50, M66, M67, M77).
